title: Complete Cybersecurity Fundamentals & Ethical Hacking Program
description: A full 20-module program from complete beginner to entry-level cybersecurity professional: networking, Linux, security fundamentals, network & web & wireless security, threats, vulnerability assessment, ethical hacking (authorized labs), cryptography, cloud & endpoint, digital forensics & incident response, security operations, tools, secure coding & AI, 10 hands-on projects, a capstone and a Certificate of Completion. Strictly defensive, legal and ethical.
outcomes: Understand cybersecurity principles, the CIA triad and security controls
Secure computers, networks, web apps and wireless — the defensive core
Identify common threats (malware, phishing, social engineering, DoS)
Perform authorized, ethical assessment and vulnerability management
Apply cryptography, cloud/endpoint security, forensics and incident response
Use industry tools in a safe lab and build a portfolio for entry-level roles
about: This is the complete TIH Cybersecurity Fundamentals & Ethical Hacking Program, rebuilt into twenty modules that take a complete beginner to entry-level professional level.

The course is strictly defensive, legal and ethical: it teaches concepts, secure configuration, detection and remediation, with all hands-on work done only in your own or an explicitly authorized lab.

Software & tools: Kali & Ubuntu Linux, Windows 11, VirtualBox/VMware, Wireshark, Nmap, Burp Suite CE, OWASP ZAP, Metasploit (authorized lab use), OpenVAS/Greenbone, John the Ripper, and Git & GitHub. You finish with a portfolio and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion.
requirements: A computer able to run virtual machines (VirtualBox/VMware)
No prior security experience required — we start from the basics
A commitment to legal, ethical, authorized-lab-only practice

faqs.question: Is this course legal and ethical?
faqs.answer: Yes. All techniques are taught in controlled lab environments for defensive and educational purposes. We emphasize ethics and legal compliance throughout, and require students to agree to an ethical use pledge.

faqs.question: What certifications can this help me prepare for?
faqs.answer: This course prepares you for CompTIA Security+, CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker), and provides a foundation for CISSP. We recommend these certifications to complement your TIH certificate.

faqs.question: Do I need cybersecurity experience?
faqs.answer: Basic networking knowledge is helpful but not required. We provide a networking primer in Module 1. IT professionals and developers will advance faster, but beginners can succeed with dedication.

faqs.question: What careers does cybersecurity lead to?
faqs.answer: Security Analyst, Penetration Tester, SOC Analyst, Security Engineer, and CISO are all in high demand across Africa. Average salaries are significantly above general IT roles.

instructor.name: Emmanuel Duo
instructor.title: Certified Ethical Hacker & Cybersecurity Consultant
instructor.bio: Emmanuel Duo holds a CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker) and CISSP certification with 10 years in cybersecurity consulting for banks, government agencies, and NGOs across West Africa. He has secured over 50 organizations from cyber threats.

🧭 Welcome to the Course

Welcome to the Course is studied in this module so you can understand the profession, learning path, legal boundaries, and evidence expected from a responsible cybersecurity learner. This lesson connects the definition to a realistic defensive decision, explains how professionals apply it, and shows how to verify that a safeguard is working.

Defensive security model
🧭 Welcome to the Course
1. Purpose
2. Permission
3. Practice
4. Proof
Permission • minimum harm • evidence • remediation

Definition

Welcome to the Course is a cybersecurity concept or practice used to understand risk, select safeguards, verify results, and communicate responsible action.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Welcome to the Course

Welcome to the Course is a cybersecurity concept or practice used to understand risk, select safeguards, verify results, and communicate responsible action.

authorization

clear permission from the system owner to perform a specific security activity

scope

the exact systems, dates, methods, and limits approved for security work

cybersecurity

the practice of managing risks to information, systems, networks, and digital services

Core explanation

Security is not created by naming a tool or control. Start with the asset and its purpose, identify credible threats and weaknesses, estimate likelihood and impact, select proportionate safeguards, and collect evidence that the safeguards operate as intended. For Welcome to the Course, always separate a confirmed fact from an assumption and record any limitation in the evidence.

  • Cybersecurity protects people, information, devices, services, and trust.
  • Ethical work requires clear authorization, a defined scope, and responsible handling of data.
  • A portfolio should demonstrate defensive reasoning, documentation, and safe practice.
  • Learning is strongest when concepts are applied in isolated labs and reflected on afterward.

How professionals apply it

  1. Purpose: define the objective, asset, owner, and authorized boundary.
  2. Permission: apply the least intrusive appropriate method and protect all collected data.
  3. Practice: interpret the result in context and select a proportionate safeguard.
  4. Proof: verify the outcome, document evidence, assign ownership, and review again.

Worked defensive example

A learner is preparing to protect a small school or business. Before touching any system, the learner defines the learning goal, confirms written permission, uses an isolated lab, and records what was learned.

QuestionProfessional answer
What must be protected?Identify the people, information, device, service, or process connected to Welcome to the Course.
What could go wrong?Describe a realistic threat, weakness, failure, or misuse without exaggerating the evidence.
What should be done?Choose preventive, detective, response, and recovery controls that match the risk.
How is success verified?Use approved tests, logs, configuration evidence, and documented review criteria.

Layered control checklist

  • Prevent: reduce unnecessary exposure through secure design, configuration, updates, least privilege, and awareness.
  • Detect: collect relevant logs and define meaningful indicators or alerts.
  • Respond: assign contacts, escalation steps, containment choices, and communication duties.
  • Recover: restore trusted service, validate the result, and capture lessons for improvement.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: acting without permission. Correction: obtain written authorization and remain inside scope.
  • Mistake: trusting a tool result without checking it. Correction: validate evidence and record uncertainty.
  • Mistake: reporting technical facts without business impact. Correction: explain who or what could be harmed and prioritize practical action.
  • Mistake: collecting excessive sensitive data. Correction: minimize, protect, sanitize, and dispose of data responsibly.

Guided practice with answer

Prompt: A small organization asks how Welcome to the Course should influence its security program. What should the learner recommend?

Model answer: First identify the organization’s important assets and approved scope. Explain Welcome to the Course in plain language, document the most relevant risk, and select at least one preventive and one detective control. Assign an owner and review date, define the evidence that will show the controls are working, and include recovery steps. Any hands-on validation must use an isolated lab or explicitly authorized system and must protect personal and confidential information.

Summary

Welcome to the Course belongs to Course Orientation. A capable cybersecurity learner can define it accurately, connect it to an asset and credible risk, choose layered safeguards, work within authorization, validate evidence, and communicate remediation clearly.

Professional habit: Ask four questions every time: What are we protecting? What evidence supports the risk? What control is proportionate? How will we verify improvement?

the possibility that a threat will exploit a weakness and cause harm

a safeguard that reduces the likelihood or impact of a security event

Security is not created by naming a tool or control. lessons.title: 3.8 Security Controls
lessons.html:
Module 3: Cybersecurity FundamentalsComplete lesson

🛡️ Security Controls

Security Controls is studied in this module so you can apply foundational security principles to assets, risks, identities, policies, and controls. This lesson connects the definition to a realistic defensive decision, explains how professionals apply it, and shows how to verify that a safeguard is working.

Defensive security model
🛡️ Security Controls
1. Asset
2. Threat
3. Control
4. Assurance
Permission • minimum harm • evidence • remediation

Definition

Security Controls is a cybersecurity concept or practice used to understand risk, select safeguards, verify results, and communicate responsible action.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Security Controls

Security Controls is a cybersecurity concept or practice used to understand risk, select safeguards, verify results, and communicate responsible action.

asset

something valuable that an organization needs to protect

risk

the possibility that a threat will exploit a weakness and cause harm

security control

a safeguard that reduces the likelihood or impact of a security event

Core explanation

Security is not created by naming a tool or control. Start with the asset and its purpose, identify credible threats and weaknesses, estimate likelihood and impact, select proportionate safeguards, and collect evidence that the safeguards operate as intended. For Security Controls, always separate a confirmed fact from an assumption and record any limitation in the evidence.

  • Confidentiality limits disclosure, integrity protects correctness, and availability keeps services usable.
  • Authentication proves an identity; authorization determines what that identity may do.
  • Risk combines likelihood and impact and should guide priorities.
  • Controls may be administrative, technical, or physical; their operation must be verified.

How professionals apply it

  1. Asset: define the objective, asset, owner, and authorized boundary.
  2. Threat: apply the least intrusive appropriate method and protect all collected data.
  3. Control: interpret the result in context and select a proportionate safeguard.
  4. Assurance: verify the outcome, document evidence, assign ownership, and review again.

Worked defensive example

A clinic identifies patient records as a critical asset, considers accidental disclosure and device theft, applies access controls and backups, then reviews logs and recovery tests.

QuestionProfessional answer
What must be protected?Identify the people, information, device, service, or process connected to Security Controls.
What could go wrong?Describe a realistic threat, weakness, failure, or misuse without exaggerating the evidence.
What should be done?Choose preventive, detective, response, and recovery controls that match the risk.
How is success verified?Use approved tests, logs, configuration evidence, and documented review criteria.

Layered control checklist

  • Prevent: reduce unnecessary exposure through secure design, configuration, updates, least privilege, and awareness.
  • Detect: collect relevant logs and define meaningful indicators or alerts.
  • Respond: assign contacts, escalation steps, containment choices, and communication duties.
  • Recover: restore trusted service, validate the result, and capture lessons for improvement.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: acting without permission. Correction: obtain written authorization and remain inside scope.
  • Mistake: trusting a tool result without checking it. Correction: validate evidence and record uncertainty.
  • Mistake: reporting technical facts without business impact. Correction: explain who or what could be harmed and prioritize practical action.
  • Mistake: collecting excessive sensitive data. Correction: minimize, protect, sanitize, and dispose of data responsibly.

Guided practice with answer

Prompt: A small organization asks how Security Controls should influence its security program. What should the learner recommend?

Model answer: First identify the organization’s important assets and approved scope. Explain Security Controls in plain language, document the most relevant risk, and select at least one preventive and one detective control. Assign an owner and review date, define the evidence that will show the controls are working, and include recovery steps. Any hands-on validation must use an isolated lab or explicitly authorized system and must protect personal and confidential information.

Summary

Security Controls belongs to Cybersecurity Fundamentals. A capable cybersecurity learner can define it accurately, connect it to an asset and credible risk, choose layered safeguards, work within authorization, validate evidence, and communicate remediation clearly.

Professional habit: Ask four questions every time: What are we protecting? What evidence supports the risk? What control is proportionate? How will we verify improvement?

Module 6: Common Cyber ThreatsComplete lesson

⚠️ Ransomware

Ransomware is studied in this module so you can recognize common threats, understand how harm occurs, and select prevention, detection, response, and recovery controls. This lesson connects the definition to a realistic defensive decision, explains how professionals apply it, and shows how to verify that a safeguard is working.

Defensive security model
⚠️ Ransomware
1. Prevent
2. Detect
3. Contain
4. Recover
Permission • minimum harm • evidence • remediation

Definition

Ransomware is malware that blocks access to systems or data, commonly through encryption, and demands payment.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Ransomware

Ransomware is malware that blocks access to systems or data, commonly through encryption, and demands payment.

threat

a circumstance or actor capable of causing harm

malware

software intentionally designed to damage, disrupt, spy on, or gain unauthorized access

indicator

an observable sign that may help detect or investigate malicious activity

Core explanation

Security is not created by naming a tool or control. Start with the asset and its purpose, identify credible threats and weaknesses, estimate likelihood and impact, select proportionate safeguards, and collect evidence that the safeguards operate as intended. For Ransomware, always separate a confirmed fact from an assumption and record any limitation in the evidence.

  • Malware is a broad category; viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, and ransomware behave differently.
  • Phishing and social engineering manipulate human trust, urgency, fear, or curiosity.
  • Insider risk may be malicious, careless, or accidental.
  • Backups, updates, least privilege, filtering, awareness, and response plans work best together.

How professionals apply it

  1. Prevent: define the objective, asset, owner, and authorized boundary.
  2. Detect: apply the least intrusive appropriate method and protect all collected data.
  3. Contain: interpret the result in context and select a proportionate safeguard.
  4. Recover: verify the outcome, document evidence, assign ownership, and review again.

Worked defensive example

A staff member receives an urgent payment message. Verification procedures stop the transfer, email filtering records the attempt, and the organization uses the event for awareness training.

QuestionProfessional answer
What must be protected?Identify the people, information, device, service, or process connected to Ransomware.
What could go wrong?Describe a realistic threat, weakness, failure, or misuse without exaggerating the evidence.
What should be done?Choose preventive, detective, response, and recovery controls that match the risk.
How is success verified?Use approved tests, logs, configuration evidence, and documented review criteria.

Layered control checklist

  • Prevent: reduce unnecessary exposure through secure design, configuration, updates, least privilege, and awareness.
  • Detect: collect relevant logs and define meaningful indicators or alerts.
  • Respond: assign contacts, escalation steps, containment choices, and communication duties.
  • Recover: restore trusted service, validate the result, and capture lessons for improvement.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: acting without permission. Correction: obtain written authorization and remain inside scope.
  • Mistake: trusting a tool result without checking it. Correction: validate evidence and record uncertainty.
  • Mistake: reporting technical facts without business impact. Correction: explain who or what could be harmed and prioritize practical action.
  • Mistake: collecting excessive sensitive data. Correction: minimize, protect, sanitize, and dispose of data responsibly.

Guided practice with answer

Prompt: A small organization asks how Ransomware should influence its security program. What should the learner recommend?

Model answer: First identify the organization’s important assets and approved scope. Explain Ransomware in plain language, document the most relevant risk, and select at least one preventive and one detective control. Assign an owner and review date, define the evidence that will show the controls are working, and include recovery steps. Any hands-on validation must use an isolated lab or explicitly authorized system and must protect personal and confidential information.

Summary

Ransomware belongs to Common Cyber Threats. A capable cybersecurity learner can define it accurately, connect it to an asset and credible risk, choose layered safeguards, work within authorization, validate evidence, and communicate remediation clearly.

Professional habit: Ask four questions every time: What are we protecting? What evidence supports the risk? What control is proportionate? How will we verify improvement?

Module 7: Vulnerability AssessmentComplete lesson

🔍 Vulnerability Management

Vulnerability Management is studied in this module so you can manage vulnerabilities responsibly from discovery through validation, prioritization, remediation, and closure. This lesson connects the definition to a realistic defensive decision, explains how professionals apply it, and shows how to verify that a safeguard is working.

Defensive security model
🔍 Vulnerability Management
1. Discover
2. Prioritize
3. Fix
4. Confirm
Permission • minimum harm • evidence • remediation

Definition

Vulnerability management is the continuous process of discovering, prioritizing, remediating, and verifying weaknesses.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Vulnerability Management

Vulnerability management is the continuous process of discovering, prioritizing, remediating, and verifying weaknesses.

vulnerability

a weakness that could be exploited to harm an asset

remediation

an action that removes or reduces a security weakness

false positive

a reported issue that investigation shows is not actually present or relevant

Core explanation

Security is not created by naming a tool or control. Start with the asset and its purpose, identify credible threats and weaknesses, estimate likelihood and impact, select proportionate safeguards, and collect evidence that the safeguards operate as intended. For Vulnerability Management, always separate a confirmed fact from an assumption and record any limitation in the evidence.

  • A scanner finding is evidence to investigate, not automatic proof of exploitable risk.
  • Prioritization considers severity, exposure, asset value, active exploitation, and compensating controls.
  • Reports should include evidence, impact, remediation, owner, and target date.
  • A vulnerability is not closed until the remedy is verified.

How professionals apply it

  1. Discover: define the objective, asset, owner, and authorized boundary.
  2. Prioritize: apply the least intrusive appropriate method and protect all collected data.
  3. Fix: interpret the result in context and select a proportionate safeguard.
  4. Confirm: verify the outcome, document evidence, assign ownership, and review again.

Worked defensive example

An authorized scanner reports outdated software on a test server. The analyst verifies the finding, rates business impact, assigns an owner, applies the update, and rescans to confirm closure.

What could go wrong?Describe a realistic threat, weakness, failure, or misuse without exaggerating the evidence.
What should be done?Choose preventive, detective, response, and recovery controls that match the risk.

Lab Exercises is a cybersecurity concept or practice used to understand risk, select safeguards, verify results, and communicate responsible action.

vulnerability

a weakness that could be exploited to harm an asset

remediation

an action that removes or reduces a security weakness

false positive

a reported issue that investigation shows is not actually present or relevant

Core explanation

Security is not created by naming a tool or control. Start with the asset and its purpose, identify credible threats and weaknesses, estimate likelihood and impact, select proportionate safeguards, and collect evidence that the safeguards operate as intended.   • Reports should include evidence, impact, remediation, owner, and target date.

lessons.title: 20.1 Certificate Requirements
lessons.html:
Module 20: Assessments & GraduationGraduation

Certificate Requirements

To graduate and earn your TIH Certificate of Completion you must:

  • Complete the lessons in Modules 1–17.
  • Complete the hands-on security projects in Module 18 (10 real-world projects).
  • Complete the capstone in Module 19 and present it.
  • Pass the skill assessments, the Midterm and Final Examinations and the Capstone Project Evaluation.
  • Pass the final Certificate of Completion assessment.

Remember: all practical work must be done legally, ethically, and only in your own or an authorized lab environment.

Module 20: Assessments & GraduationGraduation

Certificate of Completion

This is the final graduation assessment. Pass it to complete the program and unlock your TIH Certificate of Completion.

questions.question: The primary aim of cybersecurity is to:
options: Protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information
questions.explanation: Cybersecurity defends the CIA of information and systems.

questions.question: Ethical hacking must always be:
questions.explanation: Ethical hacking requires explicit authorization and legality.

questions.question: A safe way to practise security skills is in:
options: An isolated lab you own or are authorized to use
questions.explanation: Practise only in isolated, authorized lab environments.

questions.question: The difference between ethical and malicious hacking is mainly:
questions.explanation: Ethical hackers have permission and lawful, defensive intent.

questions.question: A defender’s most valuable habit is to:
questions.explanation: Patching, monitoring and documentation are core defensive practices.

questions.question: Security awareness training reduces risk by:
options: Helping people recognise threats like phishing
questions.explanation: People are a key layer; awareness reduces human-error risk.

questions.question: The CIA triad stands for:
questions.explanation: CIA = Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.

questions.question: Authentication answers the question:
questions.explanation: Authentication verifies identity; authorization sets permissions.

questions.question: Authorization determines:
options: What an authenticated user is allowed to do
questions.explanation: Authorization controls access rights after authentication.

questions.question: Risk is commonly a function of:
questions.explanation: Risk considers threats, vulnerabilities and potential impact.

questions.question: The principle of least privilege means:
options: Users get only the access they need
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits access to the minimum required.

questions.question: A security control is:
questions.explanation: Controls (technical/administrative/physical) reduce risk.

questions.question: An IP address is used to:
options: Identify a device on a network
questions.explanation: IP addresses identify devices for routing traffic.

questions.question: A firewall is used to:
questions.explanation: Firewalls allow/deny traffic based on rules.

questions.question: DNS translates:
questions.explanation: DNS resolves human names to IP addresses.
